children: Honda Motor
is pushing suppliers for drastic cost reductions as it tries to close the affordability gap with Chinese electric-vehicle makers, targeting more than
1.5 trillion yen ($9.4 billion) in savings by 2030

. The plan could materially improve margins if successful, but the scale of the demands also raises risks around supplier profitability, execution and Honda's ability to compete without sacrificing product quality.

Honda is one of Japan's largest automakers, selling cars, motorcycles and power products globally while also operating a substantial financial-services business. Its automotive lineup includes the CR-V, Civic and Accord, with hybrids becoming increasingly important as management reassesses its EV strategy.
Honda is reportedly seeking
30% cost reductions

across pressed and forged components, electrical parts and software-defined-vehicle parts. Tier-one suppliers have also been encouraged to use standardized components from smaller suppliers and increase sourcing of Chinese-made parts where possible.

The pressure reflects the widening competitive threat from companies such as BYD, whose lower-cost EVs and advanced batteries and software are gaining share across Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Honda's response goes beyond supplier negotiations. Earlier this year, the company canceled three planned North American EV models and warned that losses tied to its electrification strategy could eventually reach as much as
2.5 trillion yen
. It has shifted greater emphasis toward hybrids while restructuring its automotive cost base.
Honda's latest quarter showed the underlying business remains profitable. Fiscal first-quarter revenue rose
13.5% to 6.06 trillion yen
, while operating profit more than doubled to
530.8 billion yen
Investors Takeaway
The central question is whether Honda can capture the targeted savings without destabilizing its supply chain.
Investors should monitor
automotive operating margins, supplier pricing, hybrid sales and EV-related restructuring charges
. Progress toward standardized components and shared software could strengthen Honda's cost position, particularly after its new software-development agreement with Nissan.

But if suppliers resist the 30% reductions or lower-cost Chinese components create quality or sourcing problems, the savings plan could prove harder to realize. Honda's strategy increasingly depends on making its existing vehicle business cheaper and more efficient while it decides how aggressively to re-enter the EV race.

title: Honda Pushes Major Cost Cuts as Car Prices Bite
